# Jidoka

> Built-in quality for agent instructions. Each of the eight layers holds one
> job, and one command stops the line when a layer drifts, a job goes stale,
> or an invariant breaks.

Jidoka is an open-source standard that keeps humans and coding agents on one
layered instruction architecture. The name comes from the Toyota practice of
building quality into the process, so that the line stops at the first defect
and never passes it downstream. Instructions span eight layers, from the most
general (the system prompt, which loads on every run) to the most specific (a
checklist at one pause point). Each layer owns a single job, no layer repeats
another, and every layer has a budget that a check can measure. A defect
therefore points to exactly one layer, and the checks fail before it ships.

The `jidoka` command family runs three checks. Each check owns one class of
defect, so every finding maps to exactly one fix. `jidoka instructions` checks
every layer against a line cap and a word cap. It also fails a checklist block
with too many items and a checklist item that explains instead of confirms.
`jidoka jtbd` validates every job entry against the schema and reports a
generated block that no longer matches its manifest. Its `--fix` flag
regenerates the block. `jidoka invariants` finds every `*.rules.mjs` module
under `.jidoka/invariants/` and runs it through one engine. The engine ships
with the CLI, and the policy stays in the repository. A rule module states one
claim, collects its subjects with kit helpers such as `grep`, `scan`,
`scanAst`, and `restatementDrift`, and declares rules with an id, a message,
and a hint. A finding shows the file, the line number, the rule id, and the
fix. Every command accepts `--json` for machine-readable findings.

The standard draws on Jidoka (Toyota) for how quality holds, on Jobs To Be
Done (Christensen, Moesta) for what agents align to, and on The Checklist
Manifesto (Gawande) for how alignment holds under load.

The lowest layer, verification, uses two checklist gates. A
`<read_do_checklist>` tag wraps an entry gate, and a `<do_confirm_checklist>`
tag wraps an exit gate. One `rg` search for the two tags finds every pause
point in a repository.

Jidoka does not depend on a directory shape, so any well-structured repository
can adopt it. It defines the root files that every adopting repository has
(CLAUDE.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, and JTBD.md) and the Jobs To Be Done conventions.
A repository structure standard extends it. The Monorepo standard is one
such extension, and the Kata Agent Team runs it as a daily loop.

Install the skill pack with `apm install forwardimpact/jidoka-skills` and the
CLI with `npm install --save-dev @forwardimpact/jidoka`, then ask Claude to set
it up. Add `npx jidoka` and `npx jidoka invariants` to your checks so the line
stops at the first drifted layer. The bare command runs the layer check and
the jobs check. Only the second call runs the repository's own rule modules.

The documentation covers adoption, the layer architecture, and the checks.
Getting Started takes a repository of unlayered prompt files to a check that
stops the line on a planted defect. Put Your Instructions on One Layered
Architecture covers what each layer owns, when it loads, and which budget
applies to it. It then splits into three tasks: author one layer, write a
checklist gate, and write a jobs entry. Stop the Line on Instruction Drift
covers how to add the checks to a local script and to CI, how to read a
finding, how to route each finding to the fix that owns it, and how to enforce
a repository's own invariant rules. The layers fit inside a repository
structure standard at https://www.monorepo.team/, and the Kata Agent Team at
https://www.kata.team/ runs on them every day.
